transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Meyers: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. this is Jordan from Redwood. Samira is here from our SE team, and Alex and Ravi from product/ops. quick roll call?
[00:10] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Lena here, Mark, Priya and Evan are on. thanks for setting this up.
[00:15] Jordan Meyers: Great. agenda is a deep dive into quantization options for your 7B conversational model—tradeoffs across INT8, FP8, GPTQ, AWQ, and how that impacts latency, throughput, and accuracy. We'll also touch on KV cache behavior and VPC/on-prem considerations.
[00:30] Samira Patel: Quick note, we'll reference some internal benchmarks but every model can behave a bit different esp with GPTQ vs AWQ. we'll propose a small benchmark you can run or we can run with your artifacts.
[00:45] Mark Ruiz: thanks. our main constraints are 1) must stay within 2% drop in front-line metrics (F1 / exact match on key intents), 2) 50ms p50 latency target for chat scenarios, and 3) optionally on-prem for data residency.
[01:05] Samira Patel: Understood. real quick, can you confirm current runtime? On your infra doc you mentioned Triton + Docker on A100s?
[01:15] Mark Ruiz: yea, A100s, Triton for endpoints. some infra folks are concerned about memory footprint when using FP16 vs INT8.
[01:25] Samira Patel: Okay. high-level: INT8 (quantization-aware or post-training with clip) gives biggest model-size reduction and throughput improvement in many kernels but can cause higher accuracy regressions on certain attention heads; GPTQ is model-specific, often lower accuracy drift because it uses per-channel quantization and layer-wise calibration, but can be slow to produce and sometimes complex to integrate; AWQ (and variants like AWQ* optimizations) claim better out-of-the-box accuracy at 8-bit with faster conversion times; FP8 is emerging—great for training and mixed-precision but runtime ecosystem still maturing.
[02:10] Dr. Lena Ortiz: we've tried a naive INT8 clip conversion and saw weird tokenization behavior—some hallucinations increased on a small subset. not sure if it was conversion or our prompt changes.
[02:25] Samira Patel: That's expected. transcription note: sometimes the tokenizer interacts with quantized logits more sensitively. Two approaches: 1) run calibration on a representative prompt set and verify logits distribution, 2) keep critical layers in higher precision (e.g., first and last transformer blocks in FP16) — Redwood runtime supports mixed configs.
[02:50] Evan Cole: on calibration—how big should the calibration set be? we have about 10k sample prompts.
[03:00] Samira Patel: 1-2k representative prompts usually suffice for GPTQ calibration; for AWQ the recommended is similar but depends on response length diversity. the goal is to capture token distribution across typical contexts.
[03:15] Jordan Meyers: To add, batch sizing and KV cache behavior can amplify latency wins or losses. if you run with aggressive batching you'll improve throughput but single-request p50 can rise. Redwood runtime's continuous batching tries to respect p50 SLOs with dynamic batch cutoffs.
[03:35] Mark Ruiz: talk to me about KV cache size—quantization affects kv memory?
[03:40] Samira Patel: Good question. KV cache stores past key/value tensors; quantization of model weights doesn't change KV tensor datatype in many runtimes because KV is produced at runtime and often kept in FP16 or FP32 for numerical stability. Redwood has optimizations for quantized kernels that produce quantized KV in memory to reduce peak memory, but that can be toggled. For your p50 target, keeping KV in FP16 and using INT8 kernels for matmuls often hits a good balance.
[04:10] Dr. Lena Ortiz: any gotchas with attention implementations? we saw higher variance in long-context scorings after INT8.
[04:20] Samira Patel: Attention is sensitive. Some kernels re-order ops or fuse steps which interact with quant rounding. If you see variance on long contexts, a mitigation is to keep key layers (attention Q/K/V projections) at higher precision or use per-row quantization. GPTQ's per-channel calibration can help.
[04:45] Jordan Meyers: let's talk measurable expectations—based on similar 7B models we've benchmarked: INT8 post-training wins ~1.8-2.5x throughput at similar latency when kernels are optimized, but median accuracy regression is model-dependent: 0.5-3% on standard NLU metrics; GPTQ often reduces regression to ~0.2-1.2% but conversion time can be hours per model on CPU unless you use a GPU-accelerated converter. AWQ can be in between: near GPTQ accuracy with faster conversion. FP8 isn't widely supported in inference stacks so it's higher risk for on-prem.
[05:30] Dr. Lena Ortiz: the 2% drop threshold is tight. if GPTQ gives 0.5-1% that's preferable.
[05:40] Samira Patel: Agreed. also consider hybrid strategies: run GPTQ for the head model used in production and keep a lower-quant variant for fallback if quality drift is observed. Redwood's smart routing can fallback to a FP16 hosted variant automatically.
[05:58] Mark Ruiz: about fallback—latency costs escalate if we fallback to hosted. can you quantify?
[06:05] Jordan Meyers: rough order: if your dedicated INT8 p50 is 45ms and hosted FP16 is 28ms on our fast tier, fallback cost is both latency and monetary. but Redwood supports regional routing so fallbacks can be to compatible lower-tier dedicated nodes to limit cross-network hops. we'll produce a cost/latency matrix in the follow-up.
[06:30] Evan Cole: let's dig into conversion pipeline—how do you integrate GPTQ/AWQ into CI?
[06:40] Samira Patel: Best practice: keep quantization as a stage in model packaging. steps: 1) run unit evals on quantized weights vs FP16, 2) run an eval suite of prompts, 3) compare logits and n-gram overlap, 4) store quantized artifact with a versioned hash and label, 5) push to staging and run load tests with KV caching on. Redwood CLI can automate artifact upload and run preflight checks.
[07:15] Dr. Lena Ortiz: what's the expected runtime memory reduction?
[07:20] Samira Patel: INT8 reduces model-weight memory ~2x vs FP16 (since FP16 is 2 bytes vs INT8 1 byte) but effective runtime memory also includes KV and activations. end-to-end reduction varies: ~1.3-1.8x depending on sequence length and whether KV stays FP16.
[07:45] Mark Ruiz: are there any licensing or security concerns with GPTQ tools? some open-source converters embed code that conflicts with our policies.
[07:55] Jordan Meyers: Good callout. we typically use vetted converters and have a supply-chain review for converters. Redwood can run conversions in our secure environment or you can run them in your air-gapped site—both supported. we'll include provenance metadata for artifacts.
[08:15] Priya Singh: on-prem—how much of Redwood control plane remains external? we prefer a private control plane with optional offline management.
[08:25] Samira Patel: Redwood Private offers a customer-managed control plane for VPC and on-prem; there are two modes: 1) customer-managed control plane with our support where logs and usage metrics are pushed to customer telemetry, 2) fully air-gapped on-prem where you operate inference runtime and we provide offline tooling. We'll share the architectures.
[08:45] Mark Ruiz: For air-gapped, how do we get updates for quant kernels?
[08:50] Samira Patel: We provide signed kernel packages and a secure update mechanism you can pull into your environment after validation.
[08:58] Jordan Meyers: switching back to accuracy regressions—what do you want to prioritize in evals? exact match on intents, BLEU/ROUGE is less relevant for you right?
[09:08] Dr. Lena Ortiz: correct—primary metrics are intent classification F1 and slot extraction exact match. also user satisfaction A/B is downstream but not in initial eval.
[09:18] Samira Patel: Then we'll run per-metric delta reports and hallucination detection. We also recommend token-level logit comparisons to find layers where quantization introduces skew.
[09:32] Evan Cole: any automation to roll back a quantized release on regression?
[09:38] Samira Patel: Redwood supports rollout policies—canary with shadow traffic and automatic rollback if key metrics cross thresholds. For quantization, we often run 10% traffic canary for 48hrs with evaluation hooks.
[09:55] Jordan Meyers: we'll include a templated rollout policy you can adopt.
[10:00] Mark Ruiz: curious about AWQ—do you have results comparing AWQ vs GPTQ on 7B family?
[10:06] Samira Patel: We ran internal tests across a few LLaMA-derivative 7B models: AWQ matched GPTQ in 2/3 cases for top-1 accuracy, and conversion time was ~3-5x faster. However, on one outlier model GPTQ had noticeably better preservation on entity extraction. so it's model-dependent.
[10:30] Dr. Lena Ortiz: okay. what's the recommended path for us?
[10:35] Samira Patel: Proposal: 1) we run a small benchmark on your dev 7B—convert to GPTQ and AWQ and run the 2k calibration + eval suite; 2) compare intent F1 and slot EM, latency p50/p95 with KV caching enabled; 3) if GPTQ meets 2% threshold, prefer GPTQ for production with a fallback policy; else consider hybrid (critical layers FP16 + AWQ elsewhere).
[11:00] Jordan Meyers: who owns the benchmark? we can run it with sample data (you provide) or we'll provide instructions to run in your env.
[11:08] Dr. Lena Ortiz: easier if Redwood runs it and shares logs, but we need hashed samples and auditability.
[11:14] Jordan Meyers: fine—Samira, can you run it?
[11:16] Samira Patel: yes. Action: I'll run GPTQ + AWQ on their 7B and share a results spreadsheet and converted artifacts. We'll need the sample prompt set and the model weights (or access to the artifact).
[11:28] Mark Ruiz: security: we need SOC2 docs and network diagram before any artifact upload.
[11:33] Jordan Meyers: we'll attach SOC2 and the VPC deployment diagram in the follow-up.
[11:40] Priya Singh: about rolling updates—how do you handle scheduled vs urgent rollbacks? we need manual override controls.
[11:48] Samira Patel: Redwood Console exposes manual rollbacks plus policy-driven auto rollback. We'll demo it in the POC.
[11:56] Evan Cole: is there a latency hit for the instrumentation you add? tracing etc.
[12:02] Alex Chen: minimal—trace probes are sampled and we can configure sampling rate to limit overhead. metrics are aggregated asynchronously.
[12:10] Jordan Meyers: ok switching to some detailed kernel-level notes. Samira, can you summarize differences in matrix multiplication kernels for INT8?
[12:18] Samira Patel: Sure. INT8 kernels often rely on 8-bit accumulators or block-wise accumulation into 32-bit then cast; quantization scheme (symmetric vs asymmetric) affects bias. AWQ uses a per-block scale and small correction tables which improves accuracy on distributions with heavy tails; GPTQ tends to do per-channel scales with greedy calibration. Implementation details like quant zero-point and rounding policy can change token probabilities slightly which leads to observed regressions. That's why we recommend per-layer checks.
[12:55] Dr. Lena Ortiz: any recommendations for sequence length and batch size tradeoffs for our target p50 50ms?
[13:02] Samira Patel: For chat with short contexts (<=128 tokens), prioritize single-request latency: set batch cutoff to ~8ms, keep KV in FP16, use INT8 kernels with minimal dequant overhead. For longer contexts (>1024), throughput wins with larger batching and you may need to allow higher p95. Redwood's dynamic batching adapts to traffic pattern.
[13:25] Jordan Meyers: we'll include recommended runtime config for three profiles: low-latency chat, high-throughput background scoring, and mixed mode.
[13:35] Mark Ruiz: can you support GPU types beyond A100? Our cloud partner uses H100 and some Ampere.
[13:42] Samira Patel: Yes—kernels differ. H100 has FP8 support and better tensor core performance for mixed precision; Ampere is still best for INT8 on optimized kernels. Redwood runtime auto-selects kernel paths based on hardware. We'll surface ability to pin to a GPU family.
[13:58] Evan Cole: any instrumentation to detect silent quality degradation post-quantize in production?
[14:05] Samira Patel: Yes—quality monitoring tied to prompt sets/evals and drift detection. We compute per-prompt metric deltas and threshold alerts. If a set of prompts shows >X% degradation we can trigger canary rollback.
[14:20] Dr. Lena Ortiz: what's X?
[14:22] Samira Patel: configurable—common default is 1.5% absolute on critical metric or 5% relative on lower-signal metrics.
[14:30] Jordan Meyers: recap and next steps—Samira will run the GPTQ/AWQ benchmark, Lena to provide eval prompts, Jordan to send pricing and SOC2 + VPC diagrams, Ravi to scope on-prem network needs. We'll aim to reconvene after initial benchmark.
[14:50] Dr. Lena Ortiz: yep that works. thanks.
[14:55] Jordan Meyers: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with artifacts.
[15:00] [meeting end]
